Migration checklist

Forty-four questions to ask before you move.

Most migrations do not fail at go-live. They fail in a question nobody asked in week one — about a spreadsheet one person maintains, an item master with three rows for one product, or a price that excluded migration. Ask these of yourself first, then of every vendor, including us.

On this page

Vendor-neutral on purpose. Several of these are questions we answer badly, and the list is just as useful if you read it and then sign with somebody else — which is the only reason it is worth publishing. It is plain text with no images and no parts that need a screen, so print it or save it as a PDF and take the whole thing into the meeting.

How to use it

Do not send it to a vendor as a questionnaire. Half of it is about your own business and no supplier can answer it for you, and the half that is about them is worth more asked out loud than answered in a document somebody wrote once. Work through the first two groups yourself, with the people who do the work rather than the people who describe it. Take the other four into your vendor calls.

Expect to fail some of it. Nearly every business we have looked at has duplicate customers, three names for one product and a load-bearing spreadsheet nobody documented. That is not a reason to stop. It is the scope of the project, found before you have paid for it rather than in week nine.

Ready to see this against your own numbers?

Get a scope and a number

1. Your data, before anyone touches it

Every migration problem we have seen was visible in the data months before go-live. Nine questions, all checkable this afternoon.

  • Where does the master customer list actually live, and who may change it? If the answer is two places, you have two lists.
  • How many duplicate customers do you have? Sort by phone number, not by name. Most businesses this size find 5 to 15 percent.
  • Are phone numbers stored in one format? Ten digits, country code, spaces, a landline in the mobile column. De-duplication runs on this.
  • Do you hold a GSTIN for every business customer, and does each pass the 15-character checksum? An invalid one blocks your buyer's credit.
  • How many item codes describe one physical thing? TMT 12mm, 12 MM TMT and Fe500D 12 are three rows and one product.
  • What is the unit of measure on each item, and does everyone use it? Bags against tonnes, with the conversion factor in one person's head.
  • Can somebody tie your opening balances to a trial balance and defend them? If nobody can state the receivables total, that is the finding.
  • How much history do you actually need — everything, three years, or open balances plus last year? Eleven years costs weeks and is never read.
  • What will not migrate at all? Email threads, WhatsApp history, photos in a shared drive, a costing sheet of formulas. Get that list in writing.

2. Your process, as it really runs

The process on the wall and the process in the building are different, and the gap is where implementations die. Eight questions.

  • What does one person know that is written down nowhere? Name them, then ask what happens in the two weeks they are at a wedding.
  • Which approvals are real and which are theatre? One that has never been refused is a delay, not a control.
  • What is genuinely broken and what is merely annoying? Broken loses money or customers. Confusing the two is how a scope doubles.
  • Which spreadsheet is load-bearing? There is always one. Find out who maintains it and what stops in the week they are away.
  • What still happens on paper, and why? Sometimes a bad habit. Sometimes the only thing that works at the gate at seven in the morning.
  • Where does the same number get typed twice? Every re-typing point is a cost and a place two systems will eventually disagree.
  • How many person-days does month-end take? Measure it now, before anything changes, or you will never be able to prove the project worked.
  • Which of your rules exist because the law says so, and which because your current software says so? Few people know which is which.

3. The vendor, asked out loud

Ask these in the call, not in a document. Listen for whether the answer is specific, and whether anything at all is a no.

  • What happens to your data if they close? Ask for the mechanism. Source-code escrow is not one — nobody here can run a codebase they were handed.
  • Can you export everything yourself, in open formats, without asking? Then the hard version: can you export while an invoice to them is overdue?
  • Who answers at six in the evening on the last day of the month? A name and a channel, not a support tier.
  • How many people work there, and how many can fix your problem? A large desk and a small team that built it are different purchases.
  • What do they refuse to do? A supplier who says yes to everything has not understood you, or intends to bill for it later.
  • Which certifications do they hold, and does your largest customer require any? SOC 2 and ISO 27001 come with a report and a date, or not at all.
  • What integrates today rather than on a roadmap, and is there a public API? A named never is more useful than a vague soon.
  • Will they introduce you to a business your size in your industry? A brand-name logo says nothing about how you are treated on a bad Tuesday.

4. The money, all of it

The quoted number is rarely the number. Seven questions that surface the rest before signature, not in month four.

  • What is in the number and what is not? Migration, configuration, training, on-site visits, integrations, custom reports, the second year.
  • Is it priced per user, per module, per company or by scope? Add three people and a branch, then ask for the number again.
  • What changes the price after signature? Get the triggers in writing — entities, GST registrations, locations, data volume, custom fields.
  • What is the annual increase, and is it capped? Ask for the figure in the contract, not the intention in the meeting.
  • What does support include, and where does a change become billable? A boundary is fair. Meeting it for the first time in month four is not.
  • What does it cost to leave? Notice period, export fees, and the partner you will pay to map their fields to the next system's.
  • What do you still pay somebody else for? Your CA, your Tally licence, e-invoicing, a payment gateway, hosting. Add those to both quotes.

Ready to see this against your own numbers?

Get a scope and a number

5. The rollout

Six decisions, every one of them better made now than in the week it becomes urgent.

  • Which team goes first, and why? The one where the pain is worst and the manager is willing, not the one that looks easiest.
  • Which module first? In the order money hurts, not the order that is tidy on a diagram.
  • Are you running both systems in parallel, and until when? Parallel running feels safe and is the surest way to kill a rollout. Date the switch-off.
  • What is the go-live test? Reconciled against the trial balance is a test. Everyone has been trained is not.
  • What happens to the old system the next morning — read-only, archived, or still being edited by two people who never got the message?
  • When are you doing this? Not in peak season, not across March, and not the week the auditor is in the building.

6. The first ninety days

Adoption is where the money is won or lost, and it turns on six things that have little to do with software.

  • What does failure look like here? Two shapes: the old WhatsApp group comes back, or somebody rebuilds the old spreadsheet from the new exports.
  • Who owns adoption on your side? Not the vendor. Name them, and give them the authority to stop the old way when it gets busy.
  • Are the managers using it themselves? One who asks for the numbers by WhatsApp has told the whole team the system is optional.
  • What are people still doing in a spreadsheet in week six? The most useful question in the project, and only if it is asked without consequences.
  • Which three numbers say it worked? Choose and measure them before go-live — month-end days, enquiries with no owner, receivables past ninety days.
  • At what point do you stop and change direction, and who is allowed to say it? A project nobody halts costs a quarter.

Bring the list to us.

Ask us all forty-four. Several of our answers are no — no e-invoice generation, no GSTN filing, no SOC 2, no single sign-on, no public API — and you should hear them now.
